item.title: Palau Visitors Authority reports 76% tourism recovery from pre-pandemic levels
item.description: Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels. There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.
item.content:encoded:
Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels.

There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.

As of September, 63,948 people had traveled to Palau, meaning the country is on track to exceed last year’s total arrivals.

The Visitors Authority says that in 2025, Palau recorded the highest number of American, Australian and European tourists in the nation’s history. China remained Palau’s top visitor source market, with Taiwan ranking second.

The average visitor stay in Palau was a record 5.9 nights in 2025.

item.title: PBS Guam to host annual pledge drive Saturday
item.description: PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday. The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.
item.content:encoded:
PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday.

The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.

The annual fundraiser supports PBS Guam’s educational, cultural, and locally produced programming. The station relies on contributions from viewers, government, and foundations to continue providing educational content and sharing Guam’s stories.

PBS Guam is offering pledge gifts based on donation amounts. Donors who contribute $75 will receive a PBS Guam merchandise mystery box. A $100 donation includes a windbreaker, tote bag, director’s hat, and one year of PBS Passport access. A $150 donation includes all four gifts and one year of PBS Passport access, which provides an on-demand library of PBS programs, shows, and documentaries.

The pledge drive will air on KGTF Channel 12 and stream through the PBS App and YouTube at youtube.com/pbsguam . Rebroadcasts will air on KGTF Channel 12 every Sunday evening throughout Nov.

Community members can donate online at pbsguam.org/support or call 671-734-5483 for more information.

item.title: Regulators greenlight landmark solar project for CNMI
item.description: After weeks of public hearings, scrutiny and debate, CNMI regulators on Thursday approved a landmark solar power project that officials say could reduce the commonwealth's dependence on imported fuel and bring long-term savings to utility customers. The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission voted unanimously to approve the power purchase agreement and related contracts between the Commonwealth
item.content:encoded:
After weeks of public hearings, scrutiny and debate, CNMI regulators on Thursday approved a landmark solar power project that officials say could reduce the commonwealth's dependence on imported fuel and bring long-term savings to utility customers.

The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission voted unanimously to approve the power purchase agreement and related contracts between the Commonwealth Utilities Corp. and developer Eastern Power Solutions, clearing a major hurdle for the proposed $500 million renewable energy initiative.

The project would establish a utility-scale solar and battery energy storage system for CUC and has drawn significant public attention amid concerns over its costs, financing structure and long-term impact on ratepayers.

The vote came just two days before an Oct. 31 deadline set by Eastern Power Solutions, which previously warned regulators it would withdraw its proposal if a decision was not reached. The company said the deadline was tied to financing requirements and a Dec. 31, 2027, federal tax-credit deadline critical to the project's economic viability.

Acting Chair Bruce Camacho and Commissioner Jack Angelo voted in person, while Commissioner James Mendiola participated virtually from Tinian.

"We've had a great turnout. We've had a lot of great public input," Mendiola said before the vote. He said commissioners had spent countless hours reviewing the extensive legal and financial documentation supporting the project.

"There are no easy decisions for the CNMI," Mendiola said. "There's an element of risk on both sides, and we have to weigh the risk."

Camacho said commissioners thoroughly reviewed the proposal despite concerns raised in public testimony and written comments.

"I think we've done everything on our side to properly review this proposal," he said.

Angelo rejected suggestions that the commission was responsible for delays, noting regulators identified issues involving land documentation and liability protections that required correction before approval.

"Our goal was to protect the ratepayers, but also regulate and oversee the utilities," Angelo said.

CPUC legal counsel James Sirok said concerns raised during the review process were adequately addressed and that nothing remained that should prevent commissioners from voting on the proposal.

Following the vote, CUC Executive Director Kevin Watson said the project represents a significant step toward modernizing the commonwealth's power system.

"We're on the way to making improvements within the utilities and CNMI, and these improvements will help our customers bring us forward with renewable power," Watson told reporters.

Watson said electricity generated under the agreement is expected to cost about 18.5 cents per kilowatt-hour for 25 years without escalation, compared with roughly 44 cents per kilowatt-hour today.

While immediate savings are not expected, Watson said lower fuel costs could begin benefiting customers once construction is completed and the solar facilities begin generating power, likely in 2028.

The primary solar facility is planned for the Naftan area near Saipan International Airport. Watson said CUC hopes to break ground soon and celebrate the project's launch with the community in the coming weeks.

item.title: NPR special: 5 takeaways from a year of listening to swing voters
item.description: Every election, there is a crucial sliver of voters who help determine which candidates win. These are voters who bounce from one side to the other — the rare swing voters.
item.content:encoded:
Every election, there is a crucial sliver of voters who help determine which candidates win.

These are voters who bounce from one side to the other — the rare swing voters.

And all throughout 2026, NPR has had a front-row seat to how these folks think, listening in as voters in different swing states reflect on President Trump, the political issues that matter to them, and who they might vote for going forward.

In this case, these voters supported Joe Biden in 2020 and then swung to backing Trump in 2024.

They all participated in the Swing Voter Project , which hosts online focus groups every month. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting . NPR is a partner on the project.

So just ahead of Election Day, what have we learned from swing voters this year? Here are five takeaways:

Click the audio player above to listen to a special, hour-long discussion about these takeaways and the voters.

This special — "Swing voters and the issues that matter" — was edited by Ben Swasey and produced by Lexie Schapitl.

item.content:encoded:
There's an awful lot of movie in La Bola Negra , the new film from the directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo , who are known as Los Javis. They've made a sprawling literary-historical epic of gay male desire, one that toggles between the repressive, war-ravaged 1930s and the more liberated present day.

It's easy to see why the film has been passionately embraced, even if it falls far short of its maximalist ambitions. This is a movie of big, sweeping, often clumsy gestures, full of bloody conflict, outsized melodrama and sexual encounters that run the gamut from a forbidden caress to a Grindr hookup. In denouncing the fascism of the closet, it seeks to be a queer-cinema monument for the ages.

The directors, who co-wrote the script with the playwright Alberto Conejero, cut relentlessly among three stories about three gay men living in three different time frames. The film begins in 1937, during the Spanish Civil War. After Italian planes bomb a small village, a young trumpet player named Sebastián, played by the musician Guitarricadelafuente , makes a harrowing escape. He survives by joining the right-wing Nationalist army, which is how he meets Rafael, a young freedom fighter who's been wounded and taken prisoner. Sebastián is ordered to watch over him, which is hardly the worst of assignments. Rafael, played by Miguel Bernardeau, is exceedingly handsome, and despite their mutual wariness, Sebastián feels unmistakable stirrings of desire.

Another of the three stories takes place in Granada, in 1932. Milo Quifes plays Carlos, a young man from a rich family, who's trying to become a member of an exclusive casino. But due to suspicions of his homosexuality, he's rejected, or blackballed.

La Bola Negra is Spanish for "The Black Ball"; it's also the title of an unfinished play by the great Federico García Lorca , a detail that will come into focus later. Carlos, who's pressured by his father to return to the casino and deny the rumors, goes out and vents his frustrations at a bar. There, he joins a crowd of dancers in a flamenco-style number.

The third story is set in 2017. Carlos González plays Alberto, a Madrid-based historian who enjoys the kind of casual sexual freedom that the 1930s protagonists could never dream of. One day, Alberto receives word that his maternal grandfather, whom he never knew, has died and left him a mysterious inheritance.

The nature of that inheritance leads Alberto to conduct his own research into Lorca's life and death. Lorca was murdered by Nationalist forces in 1936, and some believe that he was targeted for his homosexuality. His artistic and political legacy becomes the tissue that connects all three stories.

Many have noted that, with its intricate three-part structure and its celebration of a queer literary icon, the film owes a debt to The Hours , which won Nicole Kidman an Oscar for her performance as Virginia Woolf . You could see La Bola Negra as an homage to that film and other arthouse classics, something that directors Ambrossi and Calvo signal by casting a few veteran actors in diva-like cameos.

Penélope Cruz steals her every scene as a cabaret singer who dazzles the troops and provides some crucial guidance for Sebastián. And it's always a delight to see Glenn Close , even if she's been saddled with a drearily written role as an earnest Lorca scholar. Lola Dueñas strikes one of the film's few genuine chords of emotion as Alberto's mother, who resents his questions about the grandfather he never knew.

With the exception of González, who makes Alberto a poignantly understated presence, the other actors are somewhat anemic by comparison. The film's most substantial story is the 1937 one, but Guitarricadelafuente, despite his strikingly offbeat screen presence, isn't a skilled enough actor yet to hold the narrative center. It doesn't help that, because of their incessantly time-hopping structure, Ambrossi and Calvo are almost always looking away from their characters and their stories just as they're starting to get interesting.

This kind of showy crosscutting is a tough thing to structure an entire movie around, and here it merely hammers home an already obvious point: that the past and the present are deeply connected. In its final half-hour, La Bola Negra makes what I think is meant to be a bold leap into poetic abstraction, but what it really amounts to is just another narrative thread to cut away to: Call it Story #3B. In doing so, a film that aspires to be a monument instead becomes monumentally tedious.

item.title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
item.description: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange. Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.
item.content:encoded:
A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.

The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.

The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."

TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.

In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.

Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

item.title: Why is the Cheesecake Factory at the center of the latest culture war?
item.description: They say there's no such thing as bad publicity. If that's true it's been a golden week for the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain. The furore began when former President Obama, stumping for Democrats in Ohio this week ahead of the midterms, joked about President Trump's White House refurbishments, saying they looked "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere."
item.content:encoded:
They say there's no such thing as bad publicity. If that's true it's been a golden week for the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain.

The furore began when former President Obama, stumping for Democrats in Ohio this week ahead of the midterms, joked about President Trump's White House refurbishments, saying they looked "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere."

The late Iraqi dictator was known for building lavish palaces, with gold walls, cabinets of gold-plated rifles, a golden throne and of course plenty of depictions of the man himself.

Trump is also well-known for his love of anything gilded and Obama joked he'd been "supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office," while also paving over the Rose Garden and "building a ballroom that's bigger than the White House."

And the Cheesecake Factory? The beloved U.S. restaurant chain was started in 1978 by David Overton, whose mother reportedly made a fine cheesecake, and now has 218 locations across the country and an annual revenue of $1.03 billion.

But it's as well known for its kitschy decor as its food, with The Atlantic writer Elaine Godfrey describing it in an article this week "as if ancient Egypt and Tuscany had a baby in Las Vegas."

Obama first made the "home renovations" remarks at the political rally on Saturday, where he also portrayed the Trump administration as out of touch with ordinary Americans suffering from a cost of living crisis and the economic consequences of the president's war in Iran.

Obama said the Trump administration had resulted in "two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption" and that those at the helm were not "serious people."

The administration was quick to respond, with President Trump defending his taste, saying: "I've taken care of the White House, I've fixed it with the finest artisans in the world."

"The White House was in terrible shape. The White House is now in the best shape it's been since 1792," he told reporters when asked about Obama's quip, adding that Obama was "not a smart guy."

The official White House X account posted a photo of the Cheesecake Factory's famously large menu, saying "Since we're talking about The Cheesecake Factory... The only thing bigger than the menu is the list of President Trump's accomplishments."

Vice President Vance reacted by accusing Obama of being out of touch with ordinary Americans. "Obama, without even trying to be, just can't help himself for being super elitist," he wrote on X.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also sought to capitalize on the backlash, having lunch at a Cheesecake Factory near the White House on Monday. He ate a French Dip Cheeseburger and told journalists afterwards: "I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," in an apparent reference to the Obamas who are known to holiday on the exclusive island.

On the topic of taste in decor, Bessent, who used to manage a hedge fund, also made an apparent jibe about the new Obama Presidential Center in Chicago.

"This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," he added.

Obama was undeterred, taking up the theme again at a rally in Georgia on Wednesday, and saying that he was surprised that instead of hitting back on his criticisms about policy and corruption, the White House was more upset about the Cheesecake Factory remark.

"The president wasn't even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison! That part didn't bother him," said Obama.

"They mobilized a whole of government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke. The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy. The person who's supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable," he added.

"The guy who's supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation. And reduce interest rates. They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory."

Obama also stressed he had been a proud patron of the restaurant for many years.

"I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?"

Later in the week, restaurants and affordability came up again. Trump told supporters at a political rally in Texas that they could spend the $5,000 he's promised every adult citizen if the Republicans keep Congress on dining out at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida.

"The problem is that for $5,000, the most you'll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert," Trump joked.

"I'm not even sure you could buy that," he said, before rescinding the advice: "No, don't go there. That's not a good place if you're price-conscious."
